result: The authors claim that no preclinical experimental approach enables voluntary oral consumption of high-concentration THC due to aversive responses in rodents, and that previous progress has been limited to mild cannabimimetic responses.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge this as background context for the study. The editor states 'As the field of cannabinoid research moves toward application of routes of administration that mimic human use, these model systems will be increasingly important,' implicitly accepting the need for such models. No reviewer challenges these background claims.

result: The authors demonstrate that mice consumed up to ~30 mg/kg THC over 2 hours when THC was formulated in chocolate-flavored E-gel, with more consistent consumption compared to CTR-gel where 41% of mice avoided the 4 mg dose entirely. The chocolate flavoring in E-gel masks THC's aversive properties.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. One reviewer states 'The authors found that they could achieve consumption of higher concentrations of THC in the E-gel than the CTR-gel, and that this led to larger total dose exposure.' Another notes 'The addition of chocolate flavor overcomes aversive reactions.' The editor confirms 'oral consumption produced THC behavioral and physiological effects.'

result: Consumption of THC-E-gel resulted in robust CB1R-dependent cannabimimetic behavioral responses (hypolocomotion, analgesia, hypothermia) comparable to i.p. administration for hypolocomotion but less potent for analgesia and hypothermia.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings. One states 'decreases in locomotor activity, antinociception, and body temperature reductions similar to 3-4 mg/kg THC when tested after 2 hour consumption.' The editor confirms 'oral consumption produced THC behavioral and physiological effects.' Reviewers note CB1R dependence was validated via antagonist studies.

result: Consumption of THC-E-gel decreased on day 3 following THC exposure on day 2, with mice consuming VEH-E-gel at a slower rate after prior THC exposure, suggesting development of aversive memory to high-dose THC.
evaluation: One reviewer explicitly critiques this interpretation: 'The abstract does not discuss the reduction of E-gel consumption that occurs after multiple days of exposure to the THC formulation, but rather implies that a new model for chronic oral self-administration has been developed. Given that only two days of consumption was assessed, it is not clear if the model will be useful to determine THC effects beyond the acute measures presented here.' This indicates the aversive effect limits chronic utility.

result: Pharmacokinetic analysis shows THC-E-gel consumption led to parallel accumulation of THC and 11-OH-THC in the brain with comparable kinetics, a profile contrasting with the rapid decline in 11-OH-THC after i.p. injection.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the pharmacokinetic findings. One states 'The authors also report the pharmacokinetics in brain and plasma of THC and metabolites after 1 or 2 hour consumption, finding high levels of THC in the brain that begins to dissipate at 2.5 hours is gone 24 hours later.' The editor confirms 'measurable brain levels' were demonstrated.

result: No significant sex differences were found in pharmacokinetic measurements of THC and metabolites.
evaluation: One reviewer explicitly requests clarification: 'The description of the PK data in Figure 3 did not specify if sex differences were examined. Prior studies have found that males and females can exhibit stark differences in brain and plasma levels of THC and metabolites... It would be helpful to describe the PK profile of males and females separately.' This indicates the claim needs better documentation.

result: THC-E-gel consumption increased acoustic startle response in males but not females, demonstrating sex-dependent effects. THC i.p. induced a biphasic dose-response in males (increased at 1-5 mg/kg, decreased at 10 mg/kg) but only decreased response in females at 10 mg/kg.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the sex-dependent acoustic startle findings. One states 'the authors tested THC effects on the acoustic startle response and found an inverted dose response that was more pronounced in males than females after i.p. dosing and a greater startle response in males after E-gel dosing.' No concerns are raised about these sex differences.

result: A dose-prediction model built from cannabimimetic behavioral responses closely predicted acoustic startle results in males and females, demonstrating reliability of the voluntary consumption paradigm across experimental modalities.
evaluation: One reviewer raises a significant concern: 'In Figure 5, it is unclear how the predicted i.p. THC dose could be 30 mg/kg when 30 mg/kg was not tested by the i.p. route according to the figure, and if it had been it would have likely been almost zero acoustic startle, not the increased startle that was observed in the 2 hr gel group. It seems more likely that it would be equivalent to 3 mg/kg i.p. Could there be an error in the modeling?' This questions the model's validity.

result: No statistically significant sex-dependent effects in consumption were found across treatments, though individual significance was observed at 1 mg THC-E-gel. Sexual dimorphic responses were not observed after THC administration via i.p. or E-gel in cannabimimetic behaviors.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the sex comparisons. One notes as a strength 'the inclusion of males and females' in the study design. The finding of minimal sex differences in consumption and most cannabimimetic responses is not challenged, though sex differences in acoustic startle are noted separately.

result: 1 hour access to THC-E-gel triggered greater cannabimimetic responses (equivalent to ~9-10 mg/kg i.p.) compared to 2 hour access (equivalent to 3-4 mg/kg i.p.), with greater variability after 1 hour suggesting differences in pharmacokinetic profile.
evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings. One states 'roughly 10 mg/kg if tested immediately after 1 hour consumption' and notes 'The majority of THC E-gel consumption was found to occur in the first hour on the first exposure day.' The time-dependent differences in response are acknowledged without challenge.

result: Consumption of THC-E-gel induced hypolocomotion on day 2 after 40 minutes of access, paralleling the reduction in consumption rate and matching the time course of THC and 11-OH-THC accumulation in the brain.
evaluation: Reviewers accept the temporal relationship between consumption, brain levels, and behavioral effects. One reviewer notes as a strength 'monitoring intake over 10 minute intervals,' which supports the temporal resolution of these findings. The parallel time courses are not challenged.

result: Correlation of pharmacokinetic findings with cannabimimetic triad results did not reveal any significant relationships.
evaluation: This negative finding is not challenged by reviewers. While one reviewer requests clarification about sex differences in PK data, no reviewer questions the lack of correlation between PK measures and behavioral outcomes.

result: The authors claim the THC-E-gel model has flexibility and utility for studying translational behaviors, can be modified for chronic studies, and bridges the gap between preclinical and human use.
evaluation: Reviewers express mixed views on chronic utility. One states 'The utility of the model for chronic consumption remains to be determined' and another notes 'It would have been interesting if this application form is also possible for chronic treatment regimen.' One reviewer explicitly states the abstract 'implies that a new model for chronic oral self-administration has been developed' but 'it is not clear if the model will be useful to determine THC effects beyond the acute measures.'
